title: SYSK Selects: How Lobbying Works
summary: A Stuff You Should Know Selects rerun (originally aired October) in which Josh and Chuck explain how lobbying works in the United States. They cover the defense of lobbying as a constitutional right to petition, notorious lobbying scandals (Jack Abramoff, the 1869 "Dragons of the Lobby" column, Daniel Webster's retainer letter, the Credit Mobilier scandal), the origin of the word "lobby" and early bribery in Congress, the Gilded Age and Sam Ward's social lobbying, K Street, the types of lobbying (direct, indirect/social, grassroots), registration rules and loopholes, the revolving door, Newt Gingrich's staff cuts and their effect on congressional research, and proposed reforms such as raising congressional staff salaries. The episode closes with a listener mail about binge listening to the back catalog.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Saturday Select, explaining that it is an October episode about lobbying chosen during election season. The hosts joke about being alone in the studio without their producer.

segments.title: Lobbying's reputation and Jack Abramoff
segments.summary: The hosts say lobbying has a bad reputation, largely due to high-profile cases like Jack Abramoff, who was convicted in 2006 of bribery, corruption and tax evasion and served about three years. They note lobbyists' feedback before the episode and that lobbying can serve a legitimate purpose.

segments.title: 1869 'Dragons of the Lobby' column
segments.summary: The hosts read from Emily Edson Briggs's 1869 column 'The Dragons of the Lobby', showing that criticism of lobbyists predates Abramoff. Briggs was a Washington correspondent and reportedly the first woman admitted to the Congressional press room.

segments.title: Constitutional right to petition and why lobbyists exist
segments.summary: The hosts argue that banning lobbying is neither practical nor constitutional, since the First Amendment protects the right to petition the government. They explain that Congress and its staff lack time and resources to research every issue, so lobbyists supply expertise, a point John F. Kennedy made in the mid-1950s.

segments.title: Lobbyists writing legislation and fundraising
segments.summary: The hosts describe how legislators need bills to build careers, so they turn to lobbying groups to help write legislation, which often favors special interests. They also note that lobbyists act as major fundraisers for the politicians they lobby.

segments.title: Lobbying pay and the size of the industry
segments.summary: The hosts cite figures that lobbyists were paid about $3.24 billion in 2014 and that roughly 10,000 people were registered as lobbyists, with the registered count peaking around 14,000 before changes in 2007. They explain that avoiding registration can be attractive because registered lobbyists face strict rules.

segments.title: Early history: lobby origins and bribery in the First Congress
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the origin of the word 'lobby', which is popularly linked to Ulysses S. Grant and the Willard Hotel but traces back to the House of Commons lobby in England in the 1640s. They describe lobbying efforts from the First Congress, including Senator William Maclay's complaints about lobbyists and treats offered to congressmen over the Tariff of 1789.

segments.title: Bank of the United States and Daniel Webster's retainer
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Bank of the United States, whose board included sitting congressmen, and Andrew Jackson's opposition to it. They read from a letter by Massachusetts Senator Daniel Webster to the bank, in which he said he had declined work against it and hinted that his retainer should be resumed.

segments.title: Credit Mobilier and Gilded Age railroad scandals
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Credit Mobilier scandal, in which Union Pacific insiders created a construction company that overcharged the railroad to inflate stock value, then gave discounted shares to congressmen in exchange for favors such as land grants. They also describe Sam Ward as the inventor of social lobbying, using lavish dinners to bring officials and business leaders together.

segments.title: K Street, post-Gilded Age rise and corporate lobbying
segments.summary: The hosts explain that K Street is where most lobbying firms are located. They describe how lobbying waned after the Gilded Age, then grew after the 1940s and especially in the 1970s and 1980s as corporations began using lobbyists to seek subsidies and contracts. They cite Northrop Grumman's lobbying spending relative to its contracts and list top 2014 spenders, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

segments.title: Newt Gingrich's staff cuts and the revolving door
segments.summary: The hosts say Newt Gingrich cut congressional staff and support agencies in the 1990s, leaving lawmakers more dependent on lobbyists. They cite the Congressional Budget Office's savings claims and Gingrich's healthcare membership group. They also describe the revolving door, with more than 400 former legislators working as lobbyists, and examples such as Ed Aldridge and William Delahunt.

segments.title: Registration rules, loopholes, and the 2007 act
segments.summary: The hosts explain that lobbyists must register and file reports, and that narrow definitions, including the 20 percent time threshold added in 2007, allow many to avoid registering. They describe the 1995 Lobbying Disclosure Act's earlier, broader definition and the American Bar Association's suggestions.
topics: Honest Leadership and Open Government Act

segments.title: Types of lobbying: direct, indirect, grassroots
segments.summary: The hosts describe what lobbyists do and the three main approaches: direct lobbying through meetings with lawmakers and staff, indirect or social lobbying through networking events, and grassroots lobbying such as paid op-eds by recognized figures. They note that corporate interests outspend public interest groups.
topics: public interest groups vs corporate lobbying

segments.title: Reform proposals: staff salaries and rent seeking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Washington Monthly article by Lee Drutman and Steven Teles proposing to rebuild congressional research capacity by doubling committee staff and raising salaries. They note congressional staff pay versus lobbyist pay and the 1970s Church and Pike Committees. They also explain rent-seeking through fossil fuel subsidies.

segments.title: Closing discussion: Veep and campaign finance
segments.summary: The hosts mention the HBO show Veep as a portrayal of Washington deal-making and say campaign finance and presidential debates are topics for future episodes.

segments.title: Listener mail: binge listening from newest to oldest
segments.summary: A listener named Colin suggests new listeners binge the back catalog from newest to oldest, and the hosts respond about older episodes they would like to redo.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information for social media and email and sign off.
